title: Tom Lellis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 31, 2007

Tom Lellis

Tom Lellis has developed multiple skills throughout his career in music. He started as a stand-up singer at age 15 and today is noted as an accomplished lyricist, composer, instrumentalist and an artist who has found his own signature sound. Tom’s recordings and original compositions have been praised by DownBeat, JazzIz and the International Association of Jazz Educators.
Tom was interviewed in Clinton, New York on July 31, 2007 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe and we are at Hamilton College filming for the Jazz Archive, and I’m very pleased to have Tom Lellis with me today. And I was trying to figure out how to introduce you, as to what you do. You do a lot of things. But I saw on your website, you said, “Singer, composer and instrumentalist.” So that pretty much —
That pretty much sums it up.
Most of it.
Yeah.
Do you think of yourself first as one of those?
I think first of myself as a singer.
Okay.
Yeah. Because that’s where I began, and really I didn’t become an instrumentalist until I was in my twenties.
Did you do that out of necessity?

Both necessity and desire. Necessity because I was on the road playing with some musicians that were truly terrible, and sometimes I would just tell them give me my first note or an introductory chord and sort of say lay out. Maybe the bass player knew the tune. And so the other reason was that I wanted to play with the best of musicians and I had to learn their language in order to keep up with them, and the dissatisfaction with the way that some people played, as opposed to the way that I wanted to hear it. And I heard my influences. The first one was McCoy Tyner and Chick Corea, and I had heard Bill Evans and so those were specifically the influences that catapulted me to try to play piano.
What is a bad accompanist?

Well either stylistically, if you’re trying to do something that isn’t in the style of the accompanist than they can take whatever you do and turn it into their style, instead of what you hope the style would be. And in essence I was very attracted to post-bop and modal. And then you would run into a purely bebop piano player who would not even © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

approach that idiom. Or a player who wouldn’t approach ballads like maybe Bill Evans, or a beautiful player. They’d play bebop against the ballad. And I’d want to be getting romantic and hear bebop. And everything — as soon as you’d get done singing it doubles up and everybody starts swinging, and you know, there goes the romance. So I was hoping to keep things in its genre a little longer. And some of those players never did want to do that.

I think being a singer can be a difficult proposition if you don’t have — if you’re not playing. Because just as you describe, like all of a sudden the trio pretty much just takes it out of your hands.
Yes.
So what are you going to do on stage?
Right.
Say, “No, I don’t want double time here.” It’s too late.

Exactly. That’s right. So that’s exactly why I started playing and then later I began playing a secondary keyboard when I could afford another piano player. I was my own mediocrity for a few years, playing very badly. But I was able to maybe not play so much but my hands are big and I can play maybe one beautiful, big change in a chord —in a bar — instead of two or three chords in the bar. And so I tried to follow Ellington’s “edit yourself,” and the old “less is more,” and just encapsulate what I wanted to say in one change instead of trying to develop a facility — starting it in my twenties, it probably wasn’t going to happen anyway.
Well I think the thing you said about being able to speak the language is really important.
It is.
I’ve worked with a lot of singers who can’t do that and it really makes it harder.

It does. It limits everyone on the bandstand. So if the singer knows the realm of the musician then there can be a dialogue and the sky’s the limit. But with limitations, you know, I tell the singers all the time that they have to know what they’re singing and they have to be the time. That’s a big thing with me. I think that singers rely on the band for the time and they float and they go behind or way behind. I think that the singer has an obligation to be the time, to evoke the time, either whether it’s a ballad or an uptempo thing, whatever it is, so say that they can handle the time. They know where it is, and they can create the synergy that everyone playing the time can create.
In your opinion, who is a good example of that?

Wow. There was a lot, but I mean my first influences were Mel Torme, Sinatra, Ella, Sarah Vaughan, Carmen McRae, Billy Eckstine, even Vic Damone, Jack Jones, Joe Williams. So those people, whether specific tunes or in general, they either swung or were romantic and were able to carry these emotions – whatever they were singing — © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
they were able to convey that emotion. And I think a lot of it is in the time, as much as in the phrasing and the notation, you know?
Did you have a musical household when you grew up?

No, but my mother, getting up for breakfast in the morning, there was a great disc jockey in Cleveland, Ohio, where I was born, his name was Bill Randall, and he played all those great singers. And my mother, who came from a kind of blue collar, no frills background, but when the radio is on and a great singer was playing, she would just light up and start dancing around the kitchen and sing harmony with Mel Torme and Ella Fitzgerald. And she would break into harmony, and I would go, “How do you do that?” like cocking my head like some dog going “what?” And so I’m sure that she was definitely my musical influence. And it made her happy. And in the middle of sort of you know that blue collar kind of grimness, I wanted to make her happy too. So I think I started singing at five years old.
Did you go through the high school chorus and all of that?
I sang in the choir but I started singing professionally at 15 in a rock & roll band and did like the talent shows, and I was in choirs and things like that.
Okay, when you were 15, what was rock & roll?

Rock & roll was like Chuck Berry and then the Motown thing came in and then I left rock & roll when the British Invasion was coming in and the Four Seasons and all that, because everyone starting singing like a castrati. Everyone sang so high. And I was getting bigger and more baritone with every passing day. And I just realized that rock & roll had gone into some stratosphere that I’d have to sing falsetto. So that’s when I sort of made the switch.
Well walking over here you were talking about working at a young age, in Syracuse actually.
Yes.
And I’m curious, when you were doing that work and then you said you had a child at that time—
Yeah.
Was there some feeling like this is a hard thing I’ve chosen to do and now I have a family and I’m trying to be a professional singer. Was it a hard road?

Well not quite then because I hadn’t been, you know the baby was just coming like and I was at this club, the fifth largest club in the country, the Three Rivers Inn in Syracuse, so I was elated to be there. And playing, at 20, 21 years old, playing with a 15-piece house band every night with some great players from upstate, here. So I was actually in heaven and just wide-eyed and coming out of rock & roll, and I had done a little bit of more night club kind of things before I got to Syracuse, but this was my graduate course in music, it © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
really was, to see Ray Charles for nine days, and to see these great acts come in and just wide-eyed.
What did you learn from watching those people?

Well that’s when I learned I’d probably have to play piano, because I saw Ray Charles come in and Buddy Greco came in and he said that he was making $1500 a week back in the forties with a hit record, and he gave it up to play piano with Benny Goodman for $150 a week. And he told me — he would take me out playing golf when people would invite him to the country club, so I’d go out and play golf with him. And he said, “What are you doing here? Why aren’t you back singing somewhere?” He didn’t want me being a house singer, an emcee, just having a little spot. So he said, “Go work, go out on the road, or go home and work a lot.” And I think those examples: Ray Charles and Buddy Greco, kind of pointed me the way to piano. Because I saw that they were great musicians. They could sit down and play — well obviously Ray — but Buddy Greco too was a fine piano player. So with that example I think they kind of got my head on a little straight that I was going to have to become a musician.
What about interacting with the audience. Did that come naturally for you, sort of — that’s a big part of being a singer and being able to be sort of a front man.

Yeah. Well I did it in rock & roll from 15 to about 20, and then when I got in the night club there, well I do remember the first time I was on this big stage and 1200 people out there in a theater restaurant, and I starting singing, my leg was going [trembling] like this, and my entire voice was quivering. So it took a little transition you know, and a little getting used to. But I think I was always fairly confident about the way I sang so if I knew the material, and you get past the initial nervousness and then it was okay.
And you would be singing cover material, right?

Absolutely. Standards, yeah, and cover material. And as I was saying Cal Custer, he was the assistant conductor of the Syracuse Symphony, arranged some things for me. So I had some specific material that I would do, and it was great.

I thought about that arranging issue when I was listening to your recording with The Metropole Orchestra, and how fantastic those arrangements are. But I wonder if you’ve ever had a circumstance where you had arrangements written for you that didn’t work and what do you do?

You know I can’t say that I have because actually I haven’t had that many arrangements. Cal wrote some then, when I was very young, and these arrangements, but I was never in a position to play with that large an ensemble usually. That big band in Syracuse, and the Orchestra were the exceptions.
Okay.
So I would — mostly small groups. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
I’d have to put down, amongst your things, that you seem to be an arranger to me also though.
I do think in those terms.
Yeah. Because some of the tunes, you’re a song-put-together person.
Yes.
You know, on some of your CDs, what’s the one you did —
“Baubles, Bangles” and “I Get a Kick Out of You.”
And “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough?”
“Ain’t No Mountain High Enough” and “Still Haven’t Found What I’m Lookin’For” from U2.
Right.
Yeah, you know I talk to Kenny Werner, a great piano player, and he would always quote other tunes in the middle of his solos, you know, a lot of players do that.
Yeah.

And I think that came with experience. You just hear progressions and chords and how things are similar and then all of a sudden you just kind of assimilate this ability to hear these things and — oh that sounds like — and then, but that was a late development, very.
Yeah. Do you have songwriting tools that you use at home to write? I mean do you do things on tape and then listen back or do computer —

Well I have the computer but I usually do that post-writing. No I just kind of sit there and play piano until I get a series, a progression or a series of changes that intrigues me. Usually the changes come first and then I’ll write the melody and the lyrics.
Okay, that was the proverbial question, which comes first?

Yeah, usually the changes, the chords. And I’ll set that up and if that’s intriguing to me then I’ll work on a melody that is hopefully as intriguing, and then I’ll try to write some lyrics that don’t embarrass me. Because that’s a big deal with me too.
Do your songs seem to naturally fall into some kind of standard form? Like when you’re writing you say, okay it’s time, I need a bridge here. Or are they just more —
Organic, huh?
Organic or —

You know that’s a good question. I can’t honestly give you an answer because I think if there’s a criticism of me it may be that I’m a little too eclectic. Or as George Bush says “echolectic.” Anyway — that’s whole ‘nother subject. So this eclecticism, I search for the not standard. You know I try to write things that maybe aren’t in the proverbial forms, or A-A-B-A. I search for those things that are slightly different that maybe I can put my imprint on that may be a little more individual. And sometimes that works, and © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

sometimes I fall back into the A-A-B kind of thing. But usually I’m looking for something that intrigues my sensibilities and then I feel that all music has to come through me to get to you. If it doesn’t intrigue me it’s going to come out at about three inches and fall to the floor. If I feel it, then there’s a good chance of me conveying that to you. So that’s how I feel about composition too, and melody and lyrics.

Have you ever written either a song or an arrangement — I’m trying to think how to phrase this — in response to something that’s popular at the time, and you think like that’s the direction I need to go here.

I don’t know about popular, but again, intriguing. It might be, I remember writing a couple of tunes that had sort of a “Birdland” kind of rhythm because I was intrigued by that rhythm. But not to — you know I have a theory about populism, and that is that if you chase that populism train you’ll never catch it. And if you did the trend will have been over. So I figured I don’t know exactly when it was, maybe in my late twenties, I said that I was going to set out on my own path and hope to intersect a trend, because I was never going to catch one. And I felt that way about it.
That’s the nature of trends, you have to start them I think.

Yeah. Or as they say, intersect it. And maybe you never will. I mean that possibility exists and I dealt with that too. So at this point, a little more philosophically, I’m just looking to create a body of work and hopefully it will stand the test of time, and I may not be around for that time, but when you look back, the great composers and the people that have influenced all of us, you know I don’t think they were writing for their specific time. They were writing what they felt and what it meant to them, and it lived because it was timeless. So that’s what I aspire to. Whether you achieve that, time will tell.
Was your mother happy that you became a professional musician?

I think so. I think that she was worried, you know, and my father always said, “Well why don’t you just like be a barber or something, have a trade.” And he was probably right, because it with the oscilloscope pattern of the ups and downs of music, I probably should have had a trade or something. But I’ve been very fortunate that there’s that philosophy of cornucopia, you get not everything you want but you get just enough to proceed, and I’ve been very fortunate in that regard.
That’s a good observation. I’m curious if you — how much of your musical knowledge and so forth came from the educational system?

Well none as a singer. I never studied — I had a quasi-manager when I was singing rock & roll who brought some teachers in from the Cleveland Institute and they said don’t mess with him, just maybe he needs some breathing or something, but stylistically leave him alone. Because the teacher will teach him to sing the way they do. But then when I went to piano I studied with Bill Dobbins, who I was working with, he had the Kent State © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

lab band in Kent State, but I was fortunate to work with him, and I studied with him and Bill Gidney, a great jazz pianist who is in Cleveland, and Phil Rizzo, who used to arrange for the Stan Kenton band. I studied theory from Phil, and then went to Bill Dobbins and Bill gave me transcriptions of all the pianists, you know Chick Corea and Monk and, you know, so I was able to use those transcriptions to see their styles and assimilate some of that. So I did study theory and some piano.
Okay. Do you have a feeling about jazz education these days?

Well having taught in the schools, some schools in the U.S., and I taught for a semester as a guest professor in Graz, Austria, at KUG there, which, it’s a very prestigious, one of the only jazz schools, maybe the only one in Austria. And I prefer the European. Because it seems to me that the educational system in the U.S. stops at — like Ken Burns’ jazz documentary, it stops at 1955 or wherever. They don’t even go into the sixties and beyond. So maybe that’s changed now or it maybe in other programs, but the programs that I taught in, I thought they were a little bit anachronistic, frankly.
Are you talking about like jazz schools?
Yes.
Gee that’s interesting you say that, because some people feel that the jazz, a lot of the current jazz teachers or players start at Coltrane.
Well I don’t see them teaching that though. I see them teaching bebop, much more.
Oh, right. Yes.
Much more than Coltrane or Joe Henderson, or that kind of, yeah. I see it, you know, pre- that.
And how would you teach Coltrane?

Well that’s a good question. I wouldn’t, frankly, because I don’t think I’m qualified. But no, as a singer, I try to give them a spectrum that takes them into the modern post-bop modal kind of thing because that’s what intrigued me. I don’t think I would have been a jazz musician had I been limited to bebop. Bebop — I don’t think it’s a great singer’s music. I think, and in fact, I feel that when — I wrote a whole article on my web site about jazz dividing and conquering itself.
I want to talk about that.

Yeah. Well that’s a big thing to me. Because I think the bebop era took the singers out of the music. All the great singers — Ella and Sarah and Billy Eckstine, all those great singers were in the swing era. And then when bebop came in it got very analytical, very — it’s a brilliant music, and difficult, but as an idiom for singers I don’t think it was wonderful because there were these perfunctory little heads that went on to the long solos. And those perfunctory little heads were nothing for the singer to sing. And I think it gave rise to a lot of singers who weren’t the best of the crop, that sang those © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

perfunctory little heads, and then did all the vocalese or scatting as the bebop players did, where I was looking for the content in the lyric and the emotion of the songs that was generated in the swing era. So then I totally — as my taste I should say — totally skipped the bebop era, I think I came in with “Milestones.” I heard “Milestones” and went wow.
Isn’t that a great record?

Right. And then, ‘cause it skipped those bar lines and started floating over the bar lines, you know, that [scats] that I just went wow, what is that? And then I heard McCoy and doing his modal thing and that was another thing that just slayed me. I just said wow, this is, that’s what made me play piano. Two specific compositions: McCoy Tyner’s “Man From Tanganyika” which I performed last night, and Chick Corea’s “Tones for Joan’s Bones.” I heard them and I just was floored. I said, so I wanted to play with them and unfortunately they were booked, so I had to, that’s when I started playing piano.
Did you hear them live?

I have, both of them, yeah. There was a great club in Cleveland that we would open for many acts, and I got to open for Bill Evans where I met Eddie Gomez and subsequently recorded with him later, and Jimmy Smith and so they all came through, and six nights, and we got to hear them. So everybody came through: Miles and McCoy and Keith Jarrett and the first version of Weather Report.
Wow.
So this was a very enlightening time for me.
What’s the first tune, instrumental tune, that you were inspired to —
[Scats].
Really?
Yes. I was about seven, eight. I started singing that solo.
That’s a great solo. That is — it’s so funny you say that, because that’s like the perfect solo.
I just loved it. I just couldn’t get enough of it.
That was Bobby Hackett, wasn’t it?
I thought it was Wardell Gray. Maybe it was Bobby Hackett.
I think it’s Bobby Hackett.
Yeah, you probably know better than I. But it was “String of Pearls,” and it was just, I loved it as a kid. That was definitely —

There’s a funny anecdote that Joe Wilder told me about that. They were playing “In the Mood” at some T.V. thing or something, and the trumpet player said, “Watch this.” And he played that solo over “In the Mood” right?
I believe it.
The conductor’s going, “What?” © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
A man after my own heart. I love that kind of thing. Yeah that was it. I just was so — it was rapturous. It’s beautiful.
And what lyric did you — did you write a lyric to that?
No.
Okay.
In fact, I have never written a lyric to a solo.
Okay. Right. That’s more like the vocalese.
That’s the vocalese, yeah. No I just write them to the heads of tunes.
What, I’m sometimes curious as to what makes you pick a particular song.

It’s just those things and intrigue me, yeah, that either they sink into my head and I can’t get them out of my head, or they’re so just intriguing, either the changes or the intervals or whatever in the melody, like McCoy’s “Man from Tanganyika” was in twelve-eight and it had these bars of nine-eight. And I didn’t even know that until later, but it was just so staccato and so flowing over the twelve-eight. And the twelve-eight was so exotic.
I was impressed by the words that you managed to articulate on that last night.
Thanks.
And I’m wondering if the story, you hear that melody, do you come up sort of with a theme or a story line and then try to fashion the words to get the story to go with the melody?

I literally went to the library and looked up Tanganyika and started studying about Tanganyika to find some material. And then I wanted to evoke the dignified primitive nature of things; how these people may be primitive but they existed long before governments, and that intrigued me. And McCoy said he wrote it about a man he met from Tanganyika. So that was all that I knew about it from the album that it came on. So I just tried to — and I really wanted to pay homage to the influences of African — the African influence that it had on me because I was very intrigued by it. And this is an African based music, you know, and it comes from there and I’m, you know I wanted to pay some respect to that and be respectful of it and so I included as much respect as I could in the tribal sense and then tried to convey that, you know, generations pass and as the generations passed it turned from Tanganyika into Tanzania and that occurred and these people probably had no idea and they just proceeded in their own culture and kept it. And to me there’s a definite dignity there that I wanted convey. And it’s profound. There was a profoundness that I heard in “Man from Tanganyika.” It was like African classical music to me.
What got you into Brazilian music?

Well I was aware of, in the sixties I was aware of Stan Getz and Astrud Gilberto and Joao Gilberto and that era of things. But some musicians in Cleveland, Skip Hadden, who now © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

teaches at Berklee, drums at Berklee, he was very broad and he would bring records by Hermeto Pascoal and when I heard Milton Nascimento and people like that, in the early seventies. And then the second tune I ever wrote lyrics to was Keith Jarrett’s “Lucky Southern” with Airto Moreira was on it, an Airto album. And it was a samba, and there’s another rhythm. The exotic rhythms — I love Brazilian music because, like jazz, it has influences from Africa, they had slavery there and imported a lot of Africans. So there was the same elements that created jazz in our country, in America, were present in Brazil with different, slightly different influences — the Indian influence there was different so they brought the jungle sounds in, but the African influence was very heavy, and the European/ Portuguese influence. So we had European influences and the African mix to make jazz. And down there those influences mixed to make Brazilian music. So to me there’s a logic there that those same elements came together to intrigue me again. And I’m Italian. So my Latin thing comes out there. I don’t like, necessarily, Italian music, but it certainly comes out in the Brazilian.
How so?

Well you know I mean the Italian thing is very operatic or very hyper-romantic, but the Brazilian thing I think, in jazz, there’s this hard edge thing where, you know, I think that there was elements where people thought I was gay because I wanted to be romantic in jazz. Whereas in Brazilian music you can be macho and you can be romantic in Mexican or Spanish music or Cuban music or Brazilian music you can be very macho and still be very hyper-romantic. Whereas in jazz there’s always this hard edge Trane, kind of hard, big, brassy, don’t get — I like the romantic. I like to appeal to the other half of the audience. And so that comes out in Brazilian music without any trouble.
I see.
That’s really it.
Have you had a chance to go there?

I have. Yes. And I’ve — Toninho Horta who is a collaborator of mine, is in New York now, we’ve just been talking, so I may go down there to record with him. But I have been to Brazil and the people walk with rhythm. It’s a beautiful thing.
I had an experience once when I was in school, at a public school, and I played the beginning of the Paul Simon record —
Yeah. With Milton or —
It was just those snare drums going. And there was a Brazilian exchange student in the class and he perked up immediately and I said oh this is real then.
That’s right.
Very interesting. A signature sound. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

It’s a very earth-connected music to me, because of all those influences. They have jungle sounds and the cuica and all these instruments that evoke the jungle and then you have those beautiful harmonies from Europe, and then you have this more primitive — primitive is hardly the word because it’s very sophisticated. The rhythms are very sophisticated. Baion and samba and the way they dance, I mean, and seven-four sambas and my God, those are very sophisticated. So all these elements, you know there is this element of primitiveness but the culmination is very sophisticated to me.
Yeah it’s interesting what we call primitive.
Yeah it really is.
But I liked your explanation of thinking of seven-four as two sections that becomes fourteen.
Yeah. Well you know a drummer explained that to me, and I went — oh the dawn, you know. It was like —
Are you influenced at all by nature in your writing in your inspirations?

Yes. Yeah. Because the more society gets away from nature and diminishes the integral part that it plays in our life, the more I want to go back to it, yes. Very much. I love to write about the wind and the water and, you know, the Emerald Forests and things. I do. I love to bring nature into it. Because that’s the more realism. That’s where the realism is. You know you can easily give emotion to those things.
Were you influenced — you have two daughters?
I have two daughters and a son.
Have you been influenced at all over the years by the music they listened to as they grew up?

Oh yes. They’ve opened me up to some — I must say my older daughter and my son too, has influenced me. My younger daughter not so much. But now I’ve influenced her. She has a compilation of Brazilian music and some of it is very earthy Brazilian music that she now likes. But yeah, to some extent.
You mentioned — I think you called it the “oscilloscope of a career.”
Yes.
And sort of tying in with your thing you wrote about jazz recordings. Has there been a time, a series of years, that were the best and a series of years that were really the hardest for you?

Working — absolutely. And that has been, you now I have found, frankly, that the more individualistic I get, the less I work. When you don’t cover and follow those trends then you become an entity that has no bearing on anything that’s currently happening. So it moves you out of the mainstream somewhat. Yet I view those times as maybe some of my most productive times because I learned to play piano and about nine years ago © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

started playing nylon string guitar for the Brazilian things, from the influence of Toninho Horta, my favorite Brazilian composer and guitarist. And so those down periods had their own benefits, even though they were not necessarily great financial years. But I can’t say that I’m happy with the amount that I have been able to actually sing. You know I would have liked to have been performing much more than my career has afforded me.
What has to happen these days, to get three nights in a row at the Blue Note for instance?

Well, you know, if I knew that maybe I could get three nights. I frankly don’t know. My business acumen is not anything to write home about. But again, I think I’ve taken a longer philosophical view that I’m going to try to create a body of work and, as I said, cornucopia has allowed me to do that, maybe not on the highest level of economic plateaus, but I don’t know. I think that the current musical scene is quite detrimental to quality. There is — I hear singers that just are abysmal in many genres, and I quote Ray Charles about rap, he says “it’s just talkin’.”
It’s just talkin’. Yeah.

And so I just quote Ray. Because it is. It’s literally just talkin’. So that has been very detrimental. I think people, there are so many anti-Christs that I have, you know, of singers that I don’t think belong in front of a microphone that are very popular now. They have, they sound like frogs croaking a song out and they have no pitch and I mean it goes from Bruce Springsteen to Elvis Costello and I think these people are frauds. Just utter total frauds.
Do you think the American Idol syndrome and stuff plays into that?

Well that’s like — well I’ll tell you a bigger overview is that I think that business has conspired to bring the masses into music. They want the masses to — you know they want you to be a singer. They want everyone to be able to sing. So now instead of to get to Carnegie Hall you practice, practice, practice, now you, like they promoted the pet rock, you just promote something until it’s so popular you can buy Carnegie Hall. And that’s how I feel about it. I feel that the quality that the great musicians that you’ve interviewed and that we all know have spent these years trying to hone a craft and all of a sudden that quality doesn’t matter. It’s not about that anymore. It’s about something else. And that something else is a scandalous scheme, a businessman’s dream — that’s a lyric that’s coming.
Okay.

And that’s what it is. I feel that all these Harvard graduates, business graduates, they’re going well why do I want to deal with a temperamental artist. Let me create Milli Vanilli. And so I blame, you know, in a culture the tallest things in that culture are the most important things. And it used to be churches and now it’s Citi Corps.
